Theme

Money, work & business

compensation noun

for a loss or an injury

also compensate, damages (money), make amends, make up for, indemnity

classical

Cic. Fam. 1.9.5: damna (Lewis & Short)
Caes. BG 6.1: dētrīmentum in bellō acceptum (Lewis & Short)

damnum sarcīre

phrase: sarciō, sarcīre, sarsī, sartum, with damnum, dētrīmentum or injūriam

make good a loss

Latin says what is done: the loss is made good. Sarcīre is literally to patch or mend; Servius Sulpicius explained the Twelve Tables’ sarcītō as damnum solvitō, praestātō (Festus, in Lewis & Short).

Other words

  • compēnsō, compēnsāre, compēnsāvī, compēnsātum — compensate, make up for, balance one thing against another

    verb, first conjugation · also used · classical · Cic. de Or. 3.14 (Lewis & Short); Cic. Verr. 2.5.33: damna ab aliquō aetātis frūctū compēnsāta (Lewis & Short)

    Literally to weigh things together. The noun compēnsātiō is the balancing of debts against credits in Roman law (the Digest), or in Cicero of one thing against another; not money paid for a loss.

  • satisfactiō, satisfactiōnis f. — amends, reparation; also an apology

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Tac. Germ. 21 (Lewis & Short)

    In Caesar and Cicero an apology or excuse that is accepted; reparation for an injury from Tacitus on (Lewis & Short).

Examples

  • summī labōrēs nostrī magnā compēnsātī glōriā

    our very great labours were made up for by great gloryCic. de Or. 3.14 (Lewis & Short)

  • luitur homicīdium certō pecorum numerō, recipitque satisfactiōnem ūniversa domus

    for even a killing is atoned for with a fixed number of cattle, and the whole family accepts the compensationTac. Germ. 21 (Lewis & Short)

See also damage, loss, wage.
